You check frames cut from an AI-made video clip before it is used in a product ad. Video models sometimes draw objects that cannot exist, such as a car with headlights on its back, a door hinged on both sides, or a hand with six fingers, and sometimes an object that turns over shows a side that is not a real side of it, such as a mug that turns and shows a second handle where the plain side should be, or a phone that turns over and shows a camera again where its screen should be. Find those, and only those.

You get frames from one clip, ten per second, in order, several per image side by side, each labelled with its time in seconds.

Work in three steps.
1. Look at the product, frame by frame. For every frame write which face of the product the camera sees. Name the faces by what is drawn on them (for a phone: front = the screen face, back = the face with the camera and logo), and use the same name for the same face in every frame. Name the parts you can see on that face in that frame, each in a few words with where it sits (top left, centre, bottom edge). Write what is drawn, not what such a product usually has. A part hidden by a hand or too small to make out is left out, never guessed. Also write which thin edge of the product you can see beside the broad face, and on which side of the broad face it sits in the picture.
2. Turns. A turn is every stretch where the product goes edge-only, or nearly, between two frames that show a broad face. For each turn, decide whether the product kept turning the same way, so the face that comes back into view must be the opposite face, or turned back, so the same face returns. Decide the direction from the motion only, never from how the face after the turn looks: that face is what you are checking, and the direction tells you what it has to be. Cues: the narrow strip of broad face beside the thin edge in the frames right before and right after the edge-only moment, on the same side of the thin edge both times means it turned back, on the other side means it kept turning; an end or edge that was moving toward the camera and keeps moving that way means it kept turning; a hand that keeps turning its wrist the same way; a product that tips over as it falls or lands keeps turning, it does not tip back up. When the cues are not visible, say unsure.
3. Then judge. For each frame, could a real one of that product, seen from that face, show exactly those parts in exactly those places? Across the frames: when the product turns, is the face that comes into view a real face of it? Do two frames show opposite faces that look the same, although a real one's opposite faces differ? Does a part appear or vanish on a face that kept facing the camera?

Decide "fail" only when you are sure something is physically impossible: a part on a side where the real object can't have it, two sides of one object seen at once, a part fused into another, a body part that can't be, two opposite sides that look the same where a real one's differ. Decide "pass" for everything else.

You may also be shown one shop photo of the product, and facts about it from the shop. They tell you what the product is and how it is built: which parts it has and where they sit. Use them only for that. Ignore the photo's background, setting and anything being done with the product; only the product itself matters. Never compare the frames with the photo: differences in size, shape, angle, distance, colour, label or print are not a fail, and the product may be held, turned, upside down or partly hidden. Fail the product only if it shows a part a real one can't have there, two sides at once, or a label that didn't turn with it.
